pages.title: India-Japan: special strategic partnership, cherry blossom phase
pages.summary: Since 2014 India and Japan are special strategic and global partners with a 2+2 dialogue, and Kanwal Sibal describes relations as in a cherry blossom phase. The page cites the Japanese PM as 2014 Republic Day guest, the 2015 visit of the Emperor and Empress, the November 2016 civil nuclear agreement with the only non-NPT country, and planned defence cooperation including US-2 aircraft.

pages.title: Japan in Make in India; Act East convergence
pages.summary: Japan takes part in Make in India, especially in defence, and is the only country allowed to invest in the sensitive North East, besides civilian infrastructure in Andaman and Nicobar. The notes see perfect convergence between Modi's Act East and Abe's 'Free and Open Indo-Pacific', with partnership in Africa and PQI and India's appreciation of Abe's new national security doctrine.

pages.title: Civilisational links; tepid relations till 1974
pages.summary: Before independence the notes cite civilisational warmth, Tagore in 1914 and Japan's help to Subhash Chandra Bose in raising the INA. After independence they mention Justice Radha Binod Pal's dissent, the 1950 peace treaty and India becoming the highest recipient of Japan's ODA, yet David Malone calls relations 'tepid' because India and Japan were in opposite Cold War camps.

pages.title: Cold War limits; Rajiv Gandhi's 1985 Diet speech
pages.summary: India's closed economy, Japan's stand in the 1971 war and its criticism of the 1974 nuclear test, with ODA temporarily halted, kept relations tepid until 1985, though Japanese firms entered the automobile sector. In 1985 Rajiv Gandhi became the first Indian PM to address the Japanese Diet, saying the relationship goes beyond the market place to the hearts and minds of the people.

pages.title: Post-1991 milestones; weak economic ties
pages.summary: Relations became meaningful after 1991 due to liberalisation, normalised India-US ties and China's rise, moving from global partnership (2000) through annual summits (2005) and the global strategic partnership with 2+2 dialogue (2007) to the 2014 special strategic and global partnership. Weak points include trade of about $16.29 bn despite the 2006 comprehensive economic partnership, with Japanese investment going to China and Vietnam.

pages.title: Business environment, future prospects, Kautilya's Mandala
pages.summary: Japan finds India's business environment unpredictable, with poor infrastructure and red tape, and Modi promised a red carpet rather than red tape, including two Japanese nominees among special economic advisors. Future prospects include co-development of defence equipment under Make in India and Japan as a natural partner by Kautilya's Mandala theory, provided the civil nuclear agreement is ratified and India keeps its business promises.

pages.title: Article 9, Abe's Dynamic Defence, Yoshida Doctrine
pages.summary: Article 9 limits Japan to forces needed for self-defence and bars operations beyond territorial waters except in peacekeeping. Shinzo Abe wants to amend it but lacks an upper-house majority, so he introduced 'Dynamic Defence' and seeks to end the Yoshida Doctrine to make Japan a normal country, which the notes say creates scope for cooperation with India.

flashcards.front: What is notable about the India-Japan civil nuclear agreement of November 2016?
flashcards.back: Japan gave India exceptional treatment, as India is the only non-NPT country with which Japan has entered such an agreement. The notes add that the agreement still needs to be ratified as soon as possible.

flashcards.front: Why were India-Japan relations called 'tepid' from independence until 1985?
flashcards.back: India and Japan were in opposite Cold War camps (Japan a US ally, India in the league of the USSR), India's closed economy was unattractive, Japan was not pro-India in 1971, and it criticised the 1974 nuclear test and temporarily halted ODA. David Malone is cited for the label 'tepid'.

flashcards.front: Which factors and milestones made India-Japan ties strategic after 1991?
flashcards.back: Liberalisation of the Indian economy, normalised India-US relations and China's rise. Milestones: global partnership (2000), annual PM summits (2005), global strategic partnership with 2+2 dialogue (2007) and special strategic and global partnership (2014).

flashcards.front: What are the weak aspects of India-Japan economic relations?
flashcards.back: Trade is only about $16.29 bn, many times less than Japan's trade with China, and Japanese investment goes mainly to China and Vietnam. Japan cites an unpredictable business environment, lack of infrastructure and red tapism, to which Modi answered with 'red carpet rather than red tape'.

flashcards.front: What is Article 9 of Japan's constitution and how does Abe want to change its effect?
flashcards.back: Article 9 limits Japan to forces needed for self-defence, which cannot operate beyond territorial waters except in peacekeeping. Abe lacks an upper-house majority to amend it, so he brought 'Dynamic Defence' and wants to end the Yoshida Doctrine and make Japan a normal country.

answers.question: Trace the evolution of India-Japan relations and assess the potential and constraints of the present special strategic and global partnership.
answers.intro: India-Japan ties moved from civilisational warmth and a tepid Cold War phase to a special strategic and global partnership in 2014. Convergent strategic outlooks create great potential, but economic weakness and Japan's constitutional limits restrain it.
body: Evolution: Tagore's 1914 remarks, Japan's help to Subhash Chandra Bose and Justice Pal's dissent show early warmth, and India signed a peace treaty in 1950. Yet David Malone calls the phase tepid, since the two were in opposite camps; Japan criticised the 1974 nuclear test. Rajiv Gandhi's 1985 Diet speech opened a new framework.

Drivers after 1991: liberalisation, normalised India-US ties and China's rise produced global partnership in 2000, annual summits in 2005, 2+2 dialogue in 2007 and the 2014 upgrade, with Japan joining Malabar permanently.

Strengths: the 2016 civil nuclear agreement treated India exceptionally; defence cooperation includes US-2 aircraft and Make in India; Japan alone invests in the North East; Act East converges with Abe's Free and Open Indo-Pacific, and PQI extends to Africa.

Constraints: trade is about $16.29 bn, investment flows to China and Vietnam, and red tape and weak infrastructure deter Japanese firms. Article 9 limits Japan, though Abe's Dynamic Defence widens scope, and Japan does not fully converge with India on Pakistan.
answers.conclusion: Japan is India's natural partner by Kautilya's Mandala logic, but complacency would waste the opportunity. Ratifying the nuclear agreement, easing the business environment and co-developing defence equipment can turn political warmth into economic and security substance.
